This reminds me...

You know those fucking annoying, awful gas can nozzles we all have now? One of the things that makes them suck is the cheap-shit way they've added vapor recovery. As you dump fuel into your car, it pushes the vapor in your tank out. Vapor recovery on those gas cans happens because the vent (which used to be a tab you'd pop open on the back of the can) is in the nozzle now. So as gas leaves the can, the vapor pushed up out of your tank is pulled through the vent back into the can. 5 gallons volume of fuel displaces 5 gallons volume of fuel vapor.

When you go fill up at the gas station, whether your car of a gas can, the same thing happens. The pump nozzle sucks the vapor out of your tank / can. We're near the point where every time you fill a tank, you're just trading vapor for liquid fuel. This is of course, all in an effort to keep as little fuel vapor as possible from being released to the atmosphere.

When the underground tanks are empty, they're full of vapor (though some tanks may be cool enough for the vapor to condense back out to liquid gasoline), both from the fuel inside the tank (obviously) and the vapor sucked out of peoples' cars. When the refueling truck shows up, they hook up a "vapor" line and the line to the tank. And they trade their fuel for the tank's vapor.

It's really satisfying to me to think about, but of course, I imagine someone at the EPA dreaming about a perfect system where you pass vapor back and forth forever... The system is far from perfect. And those fucking gas cans suck... I wonder what an expensive can that still meets those requirements would look like...

Anyway... I thought I was going to say something about the picture... But other than it being a cool picture of something we use frequently but take for granted... I got nothin.

Edit: As a bonus... the vapor recovery vent on the gas pump is what makes it auto-stop when your tank is over-full. It senses the increase in vacuum when it starts sucking up gas (liquid gasoline being harder to suck up than air) and kicks off the pump.
